docs.title: BIMopen user manual
docs.text:
BIMopen is an open-source application for building information modelling (BIM). You model the building with walls, doors, windows, floors, roofs, stairs and rooms, and the drawings come from the model: plans, sections, elevations, 3D views, schedules and sheets are views of the same model and change together when you edit it.

BIMopen runs on the desktop (Linux, Windows, macOS) and in a web browser, and it can be driven from a command line and by AI agents over MCP. Its interface speaks six languages: Italian, English, German, French, Spanish and Arabic, the last one written from right to left.

docs.title: How this manual is organised
docs.text:
Chapter What it covers Getting started Installing and starting BIMopen, the sample project, and a first small house from an empty project to a sheet The interface The application menu, the quick access toolbar, the ribbon, the options bar, Properties, the Project Browser, the drawing area, the status bar, the command line and how to move around in the views Projects and files Opening, saving, exporting and importing projects Selecting and modifying Selecting elements and the Modify tools Walls, doors and windows The building envelope and its openings Floors, roofs, stairs and components Floors, roofs, stairs, railings, curtain walls and placed components Views and graphics Plans, sections, elevations, 3D views and how they are drawn Annotation and 2D details Dimensions, text, tags, rooms, areas and 2D details Sheets, schedules and printing Sheets, schedules, printing and project settings Command line and MCP Typing commands, bimopen-cli and the MCP server for agents Keyboard shortcuts Every key and typed shortcut Troubleshooting What to do when something does not work as expected

The chapters from Projects and files to Sheets, schedules and printing are being written area by area: each one is completed when the features it describes have been checked one by one through the interface. Until then they list what they will contain.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Names of the interface are written in bold, as they appear on the screen in English: Home tab, Wall button, Properties palette.
  • A path through the interface is written with arrows: Home ▸ Build ▸ Wall means the Home tab of the ribbon, its Build panel, its Wall button.
  • Keys are written like Ctrl+Z; a shortcut typed at the keyboard, letter by letter, is written in capitals, like WA.
  • Commands typed at the command line, and their output, are written like this. Points are x,y in metres.
  • Notes, tips and warnings are set apart:

Note

A note adds something worth knowing.

Tip

A tip shows a quicker or better way.

Warning

A warning tells you about something that can lose work or give a wrong result.

docs.title: What this manual describes
docs.text:
This manual describes BIMopen as it is today, and only what has been tried in the program. When a feature is not described yet, it may still exist: the roadmap lists what is available and what is planned. The whole manual is also a PDF, one per language: the last entry of the navigation, PDF, downloads it.

BIMopen is free software under the MIT or Apache 2.0 licence. Autodesk and Revit are trademarks of Autodesk, Inc.; BIMopen is an independent project, not affiliated with Autodesk.

docs.title: Annotation and 2D details
docs.text:
This chapter describes dimensions and constraints, text notes, tags, rooms and areas with their colour schemes, legend views, and the 2D drawing tools: detail lines, regions, detail components, repeating details, insulation and drafting views. Annotations belong to the view they are made in: a dimension placed in a plan does not appear in another plan.

Before each click, every tool shows what it would make where the cursor is: the dimension with its value, the note's box, the tag on the element under the cursor, the region a room or area would fill, the line, region, component or insulation being drawn.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: Annotate ▸ Dimension holds the dimension tools: Aligned, Linear, Angular, Radial, Arc Length, and the spot dimensions Spot Elevation, Spot Coordinate and Spot Slope. They work in plans, sections, elevations, drafting views and legends. Pick the dimension type in the type selector while the tool is on; Type Properties changes the type, and with it every dimension of that type.

docs.title: Aligned and linear dimensions
docs.text:
With Aligned, the options bar offers which part of a wall is picked (Wall centerlines, Wall faces, Center of Core, Faces of Core) and what a click picks:

  • Individual References: click references one after the other (wall faces or centre lines, grids, door and window edges, detail lines, the edges of legend symbols), then click an empty spot to place the dimension line there. While you choose, the string follows the cursor. Press TAB over a wall to step through its references.
  • Entire Walls: one click dimensions a whole wall. Options opens the automatic dimensioning options: Openings with their Centers or both Widths, Intersecting Walls and Intersecting Grids. A grid that falls on a wall end adds no witness line.

Linear measures along the horizontal or the vertical of the view, between points such as wall ends: where you place the line decides which, and the space bar switches between the two.

Angular measures the angle between two walls, grids or lines that meet; more lines through the same point make a string of angles, each with its value; the last click picks the sector. Radial and Arc Length dimension an arc: click it, then where the dimension goes.

docs.title: Changing a dimension
docs.text:
• Select a dimension and click its value: Dimension Text opens. Use Actual Value keeps the measure and adds text above, below, before or after it; Replace with text shows words instead (a number is refused).
  • Drag the blue control under the text to move it away from the line; dragged back near the line, it snaps into place. Text moved far away gets an arc leader to its segment; Leader on the options bar removes it.
  • Modify | Dimensions ▸ Witness Lines ▸ Edit Witness Lines: click elements to add witness lines, click an existing witness line to remove it, then click an empty spot to finish. Each witness line of a selected dimension has a control in its middle: right-click it ▸ Move Witness Line, then click the new reference; or ▸ Delete Witness Lines.
  • Select an element the dimension measures and click a value next to it: type a new distance and press Enter, and the element moves.

The type sets the tick (diagonal, filled arrow or dot), the extensions of the dimension and witness lines (Witness line control: a gap to the element, or Fixed to Dimension Line with its Witness Line Length), the Line Weight and Tick Mark Line Weight, the Centerline Symbol and Centerline Pattern of witness lines to centre lines, the colour, the text size, offset, background, bold, italic and underline, the units (Use project settings or a unit with its decimals), and for linear dimensions the Dimension String Type: Continuous, Baseline (stacked values from the first reference) or Ordinate (values from the first reference along one line). Show Opening Height writes the height of a door or window under the width measured jamb to jamb. Radial types can drop the R prefix and their centre mark (Center Marks, with its size). With arrows, a segment too short for them has them outside, and the line runs on past them by Flipped Dimension Line Extension. Annotate ▸ Dimension ▸ Dimension Types opens the type properties of each family's current type, to set before dimensioning.

A selected baseline string shows a flip control at its origin: click it, or press the space bar, to measure from the other end. Baseline Offset in its properties sets the distance between its lines on paper.

docs.title: Temporary dimensions
docs.text: Select a wall or a grid: temporary dimensions show the distance to the nearest parallel walls or grids. A door or window shows its distance along its wall to the walls crossing it on each side, and a component its distance to the nearest wall in each direction. Click a value, type a new one and press Enter to move the element; click the dimension symbol beside it to make it permanent. While a door or window is placed, temporary dimensions show its distance to the nearest walls. With several elements selected none are shown, and the options bar offers Activate Dimensions to show them for all the selected elements.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Select a dimension: a padlock is shown on each segment. Click it to lock the segment: the distance then holds when either element moves, and a move that would break it is refused. Click it again, or right-click it ▸ Toggle Lock, to unlock; right-click ▸ Show Related selects the two elements the lock ties. A string of two segments or more shows EQ: click it and the references become equally spaced, and stay so when one of them moves. Equality display in the properties shows the values instead of EQ.

Selecting an element a constraint holds shows the constraint as blue dashed lines, unless the category Constraints is hidden in Visibility/Graphics. Deleting a dimension that holds a constraint asks what to do: OK deletes the dimension and keeps the constraint; Delete Elements deletes both. Modify ▸ Align with its padlock closed is a constraint too.

docs.title: Spot dimensions
docs.text:
• Spot Elevation: in a plan, click a floor, a roof or the level; in a section, any point. The value is in metres with its sign.
  • Spot Coordinate: the north and east coordinates of a point in a plan.
  • Spot Slope: the slope of a roof pitch in a plan, or of a sloped line in a section, with an arrow pointing down.

The options bar offers Leader and, with a leader, Shoulder: with no leader one click places the spot; with a leader, click the point and then the text; with a shoulder, the point, the bend and the text. While you hover, the value shows at the cursor. For spot elevations it also offers Relative Base: (for a type whose Elevation Origin is Relative) and, in plans, Display Elevations:: the actual elevation, the top, the bottom, or both. For spot slopes, Slope Representation: draws an Arrow or, in sections, a Triangle.

A selected spot has grips at its point, its shoulder and its text: drag the point and the spot measures what is there. A spot on a floor or a roof is deleted with it.

The spot type sets Elevation Indicator, Top Indicator and Bottom Indicator (texts before the value), the Symbol, Include Elevation and the North/South Indicator and East/West Indicator of coordinates, and the Leader Line Length and Slope Direction (Down or Up) of slopes.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Annotate ▸ Text ▸ Text (TX): click where the note goes and type; Enter starts a new line. A click gives a note that does not wrap; dragging gives it a width, and the words wrap in it. Clicking elsewhere finishes the note, and Esc ends the tool. The text size is on paper: the note keeps its printed size at any view scale.

The Format panel sets, before placing or on a selected note:

  • the leader: No Leader, One Segment (click the tip, then the note), Two Segments (tip, elbow, note) or Curved;
  • the alignment, left, centre or right, and Bold, Italic and Underline (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+U while typing), which apply to the whole note;
  • on a selected note, Add Left Straight Leader and the other three leader buttons, and Remove Last Leader;
  • Left Attachment and Right Attachment (Top, Middle, Bottom): where the leaders meet the note; chosen while placing, they stay for the next notes.
  • Paragraph Format: the paragraphs as a list, with Bullets, Numbers, Lowercase letters or Uppercase letters; wrapped lines are indented under the text.

Near the line of another note's corner, a new note snaps to it, and a dashed line shows it.

On a selected note, drag the cross to move the box (the leader tips stay), the round side controls to change its width, and the rotation control to turn it. A grip in the middle of each leader makes an elbow when dragged, or bends a curved leader. Double-click inside it to edit the words. Its properties include Arc Leaders, Left Attachment and Right Attachment, and Keep Readable, which never shows it upside down. The text type sets the colour (of text, border and leaders), the background (Opaque masks what is behind), Show Border with its offset, the leader arrowhead, the size, bold, italic and underline. Duplicate… in Type Properties makes a new text type.

Annotate ▸ Text ▸ Find/Replace finds words in the notes of the current selection, the current view or the whole project (Scope:), with options for case and whole words. Find All lists the matches with the view they are in; Find Next, or a click on a row, selects that note and shows its whole text under Context. Replace changes the first, Replace All every one, and Close closes the dialog.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text: Annotate ▸ Symbol ▸ Symbol (SY) places a 2D annotation symbol in a plan, a section, a drafting view or a legend: a North Arrow, a Centerline Symbol, a Flow Arrow, a Target or a Revision Delta, the last two with a text of their own. The symbol follows the cursor before the click; the space bar turns it a quarter, or Rotation on the options bar sets its angle. With Number of leaders: above zero, the click places the symbol and the next clicks put the ends of its leaders. The type sets the symbol's size on paper and its leaders' arrowhead; Duplicate… in Type Properties makes a new one.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Annotate ▸ Tag ▸ Tag by Category (TG): hover an element (a door, window, wall, room or area) and click to tag it. The options bar sets Horizontal or Vertical, the Leader and its length; the space bar switches the orientation, while placing or on a selected tag. Door and window tools have Tag on Placement, so each new door or window comes with its tag.

Tag All opens Tag All Not Tagged: tick the categories, the tag type of each, the leader and the orientation, for all the elements of the view or only the selected ones; only elements with no tag get one.

With a leader, Attached End ends it on the element; Free End ends it where you clicked, and a selected tag shows a grip to drag that end anywhere (Leader End in the properties switches between the two). A tag lines up with the other tags of its kind while you place it or drag it: near the line of another tag's centre it snaps to it, and a dashed line shows it. Tags hidden in the view (Visibility/Graphics) are turned on when you tag, and the message says so.

Double-click a tag to edit what it shows: a door's mark or a wall's type mark in place; a room's or area's number and name together in Edit Label Values. A tag takes another type of its own category from the type selector, and Pick New Host (Host panel) moves it to another element of the same category. Room tag types choose whether they show the number, the area and the volume. A room or area tag set to Pattern keeps an angle: it turns with Rotate, and the space bar lines it up with each wall near it in turn (Rotation in its properties). Deleting a room's tag leaves the room, and the message says so.

docs.title: Rooms
docs.text:
Home ▸ Room & Area ▸ Room (RM), then click inside a region enclosed by walls or room separators: the room fills it, around free-standing walls too. In the options bar:

  • Upper Limit and Offset: the room reaches that level plus the offset (4000 mm by default); a higher level gives a room over several storeys, such as an atrium;
  • Tag on Placement, on by default, with the tag's orientation and leader;
  • Room: New, or a room that is not placed, to put it back;
  • Highlight Boundaries: walls and separators that bound rooms turn orange, and the warning lists them.

A room placed in open space is kept with a warning, and takes its shape once the space is closed; a second room in a region already taken is marked Redundant Room and not counted twice. A number another room already has, a room lower than the computation height (1200 mm) and a base above it are warned about too, and so is a room separator drawn over another.

Walls bound the rooms of a level when they stand at its computation height: 1200 mm while Automatic Room Computation Height is ticked in the level's properties, otherwise its Computation Height.

A section shows the rooms it cuts when they are selected or under the cursor (TAB reaches a room behind other elements). A room selected there has an arrow at its top and one at its base: drag them to change its Limit Offset and Base Offset.

Room Separator draws lines that split a space into rooms without walls. A wall bounds rooms while its Room Bounding property is on. Floors and roofs above cap the room's volume.

Deleting a room removes it from the plan but keeps it in the project, Not Placed, with its data; its tags go with it. Deleting a room tag leaves the room. A room tag dragged out of its room asks whether to Move to Room.

Rooms show through their tags. In Visibility/Graphics, Rooms has Interior Fill and Datum (the cross lines). Settings ▸ Area and Volume Computations opens on Computations: the room boundary at the wall finish, centre, core layer or core centre, and Areas and Volumes to compute volumes too (by default only areas; the volume is always measured to the wall finish). Its second tab is Area Schemes.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
Areas belong to an area scheme: Gross Building (which cannot be deleted) and Rentable come with every project, and Area Schemes ▸ New adds more.

  1. Room & Area ▸ Area ▸ Area Plan: pick the scheme and the levels. Answer Yes to draw area boundary lines along the exterior walls, No to draw them yourself.
  2. Area ▸ Area Boundary Line: draw the boundaries, or pick walls; with the area rules on, an exterior wall of a gross plan gives its outer face.
  3. Area ▸ Area: click inside the boundaries. The area is tagged when placed; Tag ▸ Area Tag tags it later. Placed where no boundaries close a region, the area is kept with a warning and takes its shape once they do; a second area in a region is Redundant Area.

Deleting an area leaves it in the project, not placed, without its tags; Area: in the options bar of the Area tool lists the areas not placed, to put one back with a click.

docs.title: Colour schemes
docs.text:
A colour scheme fills the rooms or areas of a plan (and the rooms a section cuts) by a value (name, number, department, area type) or by ranges of area. Set it in the plan's Color Scheme property; (none) turns it off. Settings ▸ Color Schemes (Edit Color Scheme) creates and duplicates schemes and edits the title, the parameter, the values with their colour and visibility, their order and the ranges. Apply keeps the changes and sets the scheme of the view with the dialog open. Color scheme location, a view property, draws the fills in the Background (under the model) or in the Foreground (over the model, under the annotations).

Room & Area ▸ Legend places the legend of the plan's scheme: a swatch and a label for each value. Its Values displayed are By view (those in the plan) or All, and Columns flows the swatches into several columns. A plan can have several legends; deleting one leaves the scheme.

docs.title: Legend views
docs.text:
View ▸ Legends ▸ Legend opens New Legend View: a name and a scale. The legend opens and is listed under Legends in the Project Browser. Annotate ▸ Component ▸ Legend Component places the symbol of a type: in the options bar, the type, the View it is seen from (a wall in plan or section; a floor or roof in section or plan; a door, window or component in plan, front or back) and the Host Length, the piece of wall a door or window sits in. Legend components draw at the legend's detail level, can be moved and dimensioned (the edges of doors, windows and components; walls, floors and roofs are not), and are not counted by schedules. Text, detail lines and regions work as in a drafting view. A legend can be placed on several sheets.

A type dragged from Families in the Project Browser into a legend becomes its legend component where it is dropped; a type of Families ▸ Symbols places that annotation symbol. Create Similar, in the context menu of a selected element, starts the tool that places it with its type: for a legend component, with its view and host length too.

docs.title: Detail lines and regions
docs.text:
Annotate ▸ Detail ▸ Detail line (DL) draws lines in the open view only, in the line style of the Line style panel. The Draw panel offers Line, Rectangle, Inscribed Polygon, Circumscribed Polygon, Circle, Start-End-Radius Arc, Center-ends Arc, Tangent End Arc, Spline, Ellipse and Partial Ellipse. The options bar shows what the shape takes:

Option What it does Chain Each line (or arc, or spline) starts where the last ended; off, each one stands alone Offset What is drawn moves that far sideways; chained lines join at their corners Radius A circle, polygon or centre-ends arc of that radius (a circle takes one click); chained lines and rectangles get round corners. Offset is then ignored Sides The number of sides of a polygon

After the first click, type a length (a line, a chord) or a radius (circles, polygons, arcs, ellipse axes) and press Enter; the value shows at the cursor. A centre-ends arc never exceeds 180°: past it, it turns the other way, and a typed angle sets its end. A tangent arc starts at the end of a line or arc you click. Shift keeps lines and polygon radii horizontal or vertical and turns chords, arc radii and ellipse axes in steps of 45°, and keeps the sweep of an arc at 90°, 180° or 270°. Esc ends a chain or a spline. The same shapes and options are in every sketch (floors, roofs, regions, revision clouds, wall profiles).

Region ▸ Filled region opens sketch mode: the boundary is sketched with every shape of the Draw panel and with Pick Lines, and loops inside another are holes. Curves are kept as short straight segments. Esc ends a chain and keeps the sketch; Modify and the Modify tools work on its lines. Finish Edit Mode makes the region in the current region type, or says why it cannot (an open or crossing boundary). A selected region's Edit Boundary opens its sketch again. The type sets its fill pattern, colour and background (Opaque hides what is behind). Region ▸ Masking Region makes a region in the paper colour that hides what is beneath it. A region shows its Area and has Comments. A selected region has a grip at each vertex: drag one to change its shape.

docs.title: Detail components, repeating details and insulation
docs.text:
• Component ▸ Detail component: a 2D symbol (brick, block, timber, steel section, insulation board, break line) placed in a drafting or detail view; the space bar lines it up with each wall or detail line near the cursor in turn (a quarter turn when there is none).
  • Component ▸ Repeating detail: click a start and an end; the type sets the repeated component, the Layout (fill the available space, fixed distance, fixed number, maximum spacing), the Spacing, Inside and the rotation within the pattern. The instance has the Number when the layout is a fixed number.
  • Insulation: click two points; Width and Offset (the insulation runs that far to the left of the clicks) in the options bar; with Pick Lines ticked, a click on a detail line or a wall draws it along that line. The insulation width and the bulge ratio in its properties. Selected insulation, and a selected repeating detail, have a grip at each end.

docs.title: Draw order
docs.text: Select detail items only: Arrange offers Bring to Front, Bring Forward, Send to Back and Send Backward. Detail items always draw over the model, and a new one goes on top. Undo restores the previous order.

docs.title: Drafting views
docs.text:
View ▸ Create ▸ Drafting view asks for a name and a scale (or a custom one). The view opens and is listed under Drafting views; everything drawn in it is 2D, with no model behind it. It can go on one sheet. Duplicate View ▸ Duplicate with Detailing copies a view with its detail items, text, dimensions and legend components.

Display Model in the properties of a plan, a section or a detail view draws the model Normal, Halftone (greyed under the details) or not at all (Do not display), leaving the details and annotations.

View ▸ Create ▸ Detail with Reference other view ticked on the options bar draws a callout that points at an existing detail or drafting view instead of making a new one: its head names that view and a double-click opens it; Referenced view in its properties changes it. In a drafting view the callout is always of this kind.

Hide at scales coarser than in the properties of a section or a callout hides its symbol in the views whose scale is coarser, for example a 1 : 50 detail left out of the 1 : 100 plan.

docs.title: At the command line
docs.text: Every tool has its command: dim, lineardim, angulardim, radialdim, arcdim, spotelevation, text, findreplace, tag, room, roomsep, areaplan, areaboundary, area, colorscheme, legend, legendview, legendcomponent, detailline, region, mask, draworder, lock, eq. help followed by a command shows its usage; Keyboard shortcuts lists the typed shortcuts.

docs.title: Command line and MCP
docs.text: Everything you do in BIMopen is a command. A click on Wall and two points in the plan run the same wall command you can type yourself. This chapter describes the command line of the window, the bimopen-cli program, which runs the same commands without a window, and the MCP server, through which an AI agent can model, check and render a project.

docs.title: The command line in the window
docs.text:
The command line sits under the drawing area. Its upper part is the log; its last row is where you type.

  • You do not need to click it first: whatever you type while no other field is being edited goes there.
  • Enter runs the line. The command is echoed in the log after a >, followed by its result; an error is shown in red and changes nothing.
  • Up and Down bring back the lines typed before.
  • On the left of the row, the prompt says what is expected: Command: when no tool is active, or the request of the active tool, such as WALL next point [Esc to finish]:.
  • help lists every command with a line of description; help wall shows the usage of one. ? ▸ Commands in the title bar does the same as help.

docs.title: Typed shortcuts start the tools
docs.text:
A command typed without arguments starts the interactive tool, as if you clicked its button: WA (or wall) starts the wall tool, DR the door tool, VG opens Visibility/Graphics. The same command with arguments does the work at once, without the tool: wall 0,0 5,0 draws a wall from the origin to 5 m along x.

Command names, their short forms and their arguments are the same in every language of the interface; most also accept an Italian name, such as muro for wall. Parameter names, type names and view names follow the language of the interface: in English you type set Unconnected Height 2.7m, in Italian set Altezza non collegata 2.7m. The keyboard shortcuts chapter lists every short form.

docs.title: Points and lengths
docs.text:
You type It means 3,4 The point x = 3 m, y = 4 m @2,0 2 m along x and 0 along y from the previous point @4<90 4 m from the previous point, at 90° (angles counter-clockwise from the x axis) 2.7m, 270cm, 2700mm A length with its unit 2.7 or 2,7 A length in metres: at the command line a number without unit is in metres

For example, wall 0,0 @6,0 @4<90 0,4 c draws a 6 × 4 m rectangle; the final c closes it.

Warning

At the command line set Unconnected Height 2700 means 2700 metres. Write the unit: 2700mm. In the Properties palette, instead, a number without unit is in the project's units, millimetres in a new project.

docs.title: Arguments in JSON
docs.text:
Every command also takes its arguments as a JSON object, which gives access to all its options. The usage line of help lists them:

wall 0,0 10,0 {"height":3.2,"location":"Linea d'asse del muro"}
roof walls {"slope":30,"overhang":0.5}
sheet A102 Plans {"title_block":"A3"}
export doors.csv {"schedule":"doors"}

docs.title: Commands you will use often
docs.text:
Command What it does new, sample A new project, the sample project open house.bimopen, save house.bimopen Opens and saves a project undo, redo Undoes and redoes the last change view 3d, view Ground Floor Opens the default 3D view, or the plan of a level wall, door, window, floor, roof Model elements: see the usage with help select walls, select all, deselect Selects by category, everything, nothing set <parameter> <value> Sets a parameter of the selection, as in the Properties palette type <type name> Changes the type of the selection, or of the next element move 1,0, copy 0,3, rotate 90 Modifies the selection delete Deletes the selection list walls, params 102, info Lists elements, the parameters of one, a summary of the project schedule doors Shows a schedule at the command line export house.ifc Exports IFC, SVG, PNG or CSV, by the file's extension

Every element has a number, its id, shown in brackets after it is created: Door «Single swing door 80x210» in wall 102 (106). Commands accept it where they need an element: params 106, delete 106.

docs.title: bimopen-cli
docs.text:
bimopen-cli runs BIMopen without a window: to convert files, to build a project from a script, to check a model, or to serve agents over MCP. Build it with cargo build --release -p bimopen-cli.

bimopen-cli info <file>
bimopen-cli convert <in> <out> [--level NAME] [--view 3d] [--schedule walls|doors|windows|floors|rooms|materials]
bimopen-cli run [<file> | --sample] [--cmd LINE]… [--script FILE] [--save FILE] [--export FILE]…
bimopen-cli commands
bimopen-cli mcp [<file> | --sample]
Subcommand What it does info <file> A summary of the project and, in JSON, its levels, element counts and active view convert <in> <out> Opens <in> (.bimopen or .rvt) and writes <out>: .ifc, .svg or .png of a plan (the lowest level, or --level), .png of the 3D view (--view 3d), .csv of a schedule (--schedule), or .bimopen run Opens a file, the sample, or a new project, then runs the options in order: --cmd one line, --script a file of lines (empty lines and lines starting with # are skipped), --save and --export a file commands Every command, with its description and usage mcp The MCP server on standard input and output --version The version

The messages are in the language of the environment variable BIMOPEN_LANG (it, en, de, fr, es, ar), or of the system (LANG), or Italian. bimopen-cli ends with code 0 when everything worked, 1 when a command failed (the message says which), and 2 when the arguments are wrong (it prints the usage).

export BIMOPEN_LANG=en
bimopen-cli run --script house.txt --save house.bimopen --export house.ifc
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen plan.svg
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen doors.csv --schedule doors
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen first.png --level "First Floor"
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen house-3d.png --view 3d
bimopen-cli convert project.rvt project.bimopen

A script is a text file with one command per line, exactly as typed at the command line:

# a small house
wall 0,0 10,0 10,6 0,6 c
door 5,0
window 10,3
floor walls
roof walls

The schedules are written as CSV with ; between the columns, the headings in the language of the messages and a total row at the end.

docs.title: MCP: BIMopen for AI agents
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI agent use programs as tools. bimopen-cli mcp is an MCP server: it speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 on standard input and output, one message per line, and keeps one project open for the whole conversation. Without a file it starts from a new project; --sample starts from the sample house.

To add it to an agent, give the agent the command to start. For example, in Claude Code:

claude mcp add bimopen -- bimopen-cli mcp --sample

or, in a client configured with JSON:

{ "mcpServers": { "bimopen": { "command": "bimopen-cli", "args": ["mcp", "--sample"] } } }

The server offers seven tools:

Tool Arguments What it does command_line line Types a line at the command line, exactly as a person would execute command, args Runs a command with its arguments in JSON inspect_model – A summary: levels, element counts, active view, selection query_elements category (optional) The elements, with id, category and name: walls, doors, windows, floors, rooms, roomseps, grids, levels, types get_params id Every parameter of an element schedule kind A schedule: walls, doors, windows, floors, rooms or materials render view, width, height, yaw, pitch A PNG image of a view: 3d, the name of a level for its plan, of a section, elevation, callout or drafting view, or the number or name of a sheet; yaw and pitch turn the 3D camera, in degrees

The answers carry the message of the command and, when there is one, its data in JSON, such as the ids of the elements created. An agent can check its own work by asking for a render.

Tip

Ask the agent to render the plan and the 3D view after each step: it sees what it built and corrects itself.

docs.title: Sheets, schedules and printing
docs.text: This chapter describes how the project is documented: sheets and their title blocks, the views placed on them, revisions, schedules, printed drawings and exported images.

docs.title: Sheets
docs.text: A sheet is a drawing to print: a title block and the views placed on it. Sheets are listed under Sheets (all) in the Project Browser, by number.

docs.title: Creating a sheet
docs.text:
View ➤ Sheet Composition ➤ Sheet opens New Sheet: choose a title block (its paper size is shown), None, or one of the placeholder sheets of the sheet list. OK creates the sheet with the next free number (A101, A102…) and opens it.

Right-click a sheet in the Project Browser ➤ Rename… to change its number and name in Sheet Title. The other parameters of the sheet are in the Properties palette: Sheet Number, Sheet Name, Sheet Issue Date, Drawn By, Checked By, Designed By, Approved By, Appears In Sheet List, its guide grid and its revisions. Several sheets picked together in the Project Browser (with Ctrl or Shift) are changed together: the palette shows the values they share.

Manage ➤ Settings ➤ Project information sets what every sheet shows: Project Issue Date, Project Status, Client Name, Project Address, Project Name and Project Number.

docs.title: Title blocks
docs.text:
The title block shows the project's information, the sheet's number and name, the people and the dates, the current revision and the scale (As indicated when the views have different scales); above it, a table lists the sheet's revisions with their number, description and date. A double click on one of its fields types the value in place.

  • Click a line of the title block to pick it: the type selector changes it to another paper size, Del removes it (the sheet and its views stay).
  • View ➤ Sheet Composition ➤ Title Block inserts one on the open sheet: choose it in the type selector, its frame follows the cursor, click to place it.
  • Edit Type shows its Sheet width and Sheet height; Duplicate… makes a new paper size.

docs.title: Views on sheets
docs.text:
Drag a view from the Project Browser onto the sheet, or use View ➤ Sheet Composition ➤ View (Views, then Add View to Sheet): the view follows the cursor at its scale, and a click places it as a viewport. A view goes on one sheet only; a schedule on several.

A picked viewport:

  • moves with the mouse or the arrow keys, unless it is pinned (Pin); near another view, its title lines up with the other's and a dashed line shows it;
  • has its View Scale, its Title on Sheet (also typed by double-clicking the title) and its Rotation on Sheet (90° clockwise or counter-clockwise; the title stays horizontal);
  • shows the end of its title line, which can be dragged;
  • takes a viewport type from the type selector: No Title, Title w/ Line or Title w/o Line, or a type of your own (Show Title, Show Extension Line, line weight, colour and pattern of the line);
  • leaves the sheet with Del; the view stays in the project.

Activate View (on the Modify | Viewports tab or the right button) edits the view where it is on the sheet, the rest of the sheet in halftone; Deactivate View goes back to the sheet. A view turned on its sheet cannot be activated: take its rotation off first. A double click on a view opens it in its own window.

docs.title: Guide grids
docs.text: View ➤ Sheet Composition ➤ Guide Grid asks for a name and covers the sheet with a grid. Pick it to drag its corners or to set its Guide spacing; the sheet's Guide Grid parameter shows the same grid on other sheets, or none. Views dragged near the grid's lines snap onto them. The grid is never printed.

docs.title: Sheet list
docs.text: View ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Sheet List makes a schedule of the sheets: number, name and any other field. Sheets with Appears In Sheet List unticked are left out. Rows ➤ New adds a placeholder sheet: a row that is not a sheet yet and is not in the Project Browser. Filter placeholder sheets shows every row, hides the placeholders or shows only them. A placeholder chosen in New Sheet becomes a real sheet.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
View ➤ Sheet Composition ➤ Sheet Issues/Revisions lists the revisions of the project, one per row: Sequence, Numbering (Numeric, Alphabetic or none), Date, Description, Issued, Issued to, Issued by and Show. Add adds one; a row picked by its sequence number is merged into the one above or below (its clouds go with it) or moved up and down. Numbering is Per Project or Per Sheet (the place of the revision among the sheet's revisions); Alphabetical order ➤ Options… sets the letters used. An issued revision cannot be changed, and neither can its clouds, until Issued is unticked.

Annotate ➤ Detail ➤ Revision Cloud draws a cloud in a plan, a section, a drafting view or on a sheet: sketch closed loops with the shapes of the Draw panel, then Finish Edit Mode; a selected cloud's Edit Sketch opens them again, unless its revision is issued. The cloud takes the latest revision not issued; picked, it shows its Revision (to change), its number, date and people, its Mark and Comments. Show of a revision draws its clouds and tags, keeps them but does not draw them, or hides them.

A sheet lists the revisions of the clouds of its views and of its own clouds. Its Revisions on Sheet (in the Properties palette, Edit…) adds other revisions to the list.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text: A schedule is a table of the elements of the model, and a view like the others: it opens in a window of the drawing area, is tiled, cascaded and switched with plans, sections and 3D views, and is listed under Schedules/Quantities in the Project Browser. It follows every change of the model at once, and every change made in it changes the model.

docs.title: Creating a schedule
docs.text: View ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Schedule/Quantities opens New Schedule: choose a category, a name (the default follows the category until one is typed) and Schedule building components or Schedule keys. OK opens Schedule Properties; its second OK creates the schedule and opens its view. Material Takeoff in the same menu lists the materials of the layers of walls, floors and roofs.

docs.title: Schedule Properties
docs.text:
The dialog opens again from the Properties palette of the schedule (each tab has its Edit… button) or from the right button on the schedule in the Project Browser. Its tabs:

Tab What it sets Fields The columns, chosen from Available fields: and put in order; the fields of the rooms the elements are in; Add Parameter… for a project or shared parameter; Calculated Value… for a formula (with + - * / ^, sqrt, round, IF, AND, OR, NOT and units) or a percentage Filter Up to four criteria, all of which an element must meet Sorting/Grouping Up to four sort levels, each with Header, footer and Blank line; the grand totals; Itemize every instance (off: one row per type) Formatting Per field: heading, orientation, alignment, hidden field, Format… (units, rounding, symbol), totals and Conditional Format… (a background colour where a value meets a test) Appearance Grid lines and outline with their line styles, the title and the column headers, a blank row, Header text and Body text (size, Bold, Italic); shown when the schedule is on a sheet

docs.title: Working in a schedule view
docs.text:
• A cell edits the element, or its type for a type parameter; every edit is one step of undo.
  • A row selects its elements in every view. Highlight in model on the Modify | Schedule/Quantities tab opens Show Elements in View, which brings a plan forward framed on them; Show goes on to the next view.
  • Rows ➤ Delete deletes the elements of the selected rows, after asking.
  • Headings picked together are joined under a common heading with Group, and parted with Ungroup; Hide column and Unhide all columns work on the column picked.

docs.title: Schedules on sheets
docs.text: Drag a schedule from the Project Browser onto a sheet. Selected on the sheet, it shows its controls: the Z on the right edge of a segment splits it in two, the arrow in the middle of a segment moves it (dropped on the segment beside it, the two join), the dot at the bottom of a segment moves its last row, and the triangles at the top of the columns set their widths. A double click, or Edit Schedule on the right button, opens the schedule view. The same schedule can go on several sheets.

docs.title: Key schedules and material takeoffs
docs.text:
A key schedule (Schedule keys in New Schedule) defines named sets of values, one row per key, added and deleted with Rows. Its Key Name becomes a parameter of the category: choosing a key for an element gives it all the values of that row.

A material takeoff lists, for each element, the materials of its layers with their area and volume; its fields can be sorted, grouped and totalled like any other.

docs.title: Project and shared parameters
docs.text:
Manage ➤ Settings ➤ Project Parameters adds parameters to the elements of some categories, or to their types, with a name, a type of value and the group they show in the Properties palette.

Manage ➤ Settings ➤ Shared Parameters opens Edit Shared Parameters: the shared parameter file in use (Browse…, Create…), its groups and the parameters of each group. A shared parameter keeps its name and type, and has an identifier of its own, so that several projects add the same parameter. In Parameter Properties, choose Shared parameter and Select… to add one to the project; Export… writes a shared parameter of the project back to the file.

docs.title: Exporting and reusing schedules
docs.text:
• Application menu ➤ Export ➤ Reports ➤ Schedule… writes the schedule as delimited text: Export Schedule sets the field delimiter, the text qualifier and which headings and group rows go in the file.
  • Create view template from view… on the right button of a schedule makes a view template with its fields, filter, sorting, formatting and appearance; Apply view template… gives them to another schedule.
  • Save to New File… on the right button writes the schedule's setup, without the elements, to a file of its own. Insert ➤ Import ➤ Insert from File ➤ Insert Views from File… brings the schedules of another project into this one, with their project parameters.

docs.title: Printing
docs.text: Printing writes PDF files: on the desktop they are saved where you choose, in the browser they are downloaded.

docs.title: The Print dialog
docs.text:
Ctrl+P, or application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print…, opens Print:

  • File: the name of the file and, when several views or sheets are printed, Combine multiple selected views/sheets into a single file (one page each) or Create separate files (one file each, named after the sheet or view).
  • Print Range: Current window, Visible portion of current window (only what the window shows), or Selected views/sheets with Select….
  • Reverse print order prints the last page first.
  • Settings: the print settings in use, changed with Settings…; Preview shows the pages.

Plans, sections, elevations, drafting views and sheets print as drawings; the 3D window prints as an image of the view; a schedule prints its table on a page. The page is always white, elements hidden temporarily in a window are printed, and each printed sheet carries the date and time of the print.

docs.title: View/sheet sets
docs.text: Select… opens View/Sheet Set: tick the sheets and views to print (Show sheets, views or both; Check all, Check none). A set is saved by name with Save As… and kept in the project; Save, Reset, Rename… and Delete manage the saved sets, and the name list picks one again.

docs.title: Print Setup
docs.text:
application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print Setup…, or Settings… in Print, sets:

Setting What it does Size and Orientation The paper (A0 to A4, or the sheet's own size) and its orientation Paper Placement Center, or an offset from the lower-left corner Hidden line views Vector Processing or Raster Processing (the pages as images, at the raster quality chosen) Zoom Fit to page, or a percentage of the real size Colors Black Lines, Grayscale or Colour Options Show view links in blue, Hide unreferenced view tags, Hide crop boundaries, Replace halftone with thin lines

Settings are saved by name with Save As…, and kept in the project. Closing the dialog after changing saved settings asks whether to save the changes; No keeps them for this session only.

docs.title: Print Preview
docs.text: application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print Preview, or Preview in Print, shows the pages as they will print, in their colours: Previous Page and Next Page go through them, the wheel zooms and dragging pans; Print… prints, Close goes back.

docs.title: Exporting images
docs.text:
application menu ➤ Export ➤ Images and animations ➤ Image… opens Export Image:

  • the file name and the Export Range: the current window, its visible portion, or the views and sheets chosen (one file each);
  • the Image Size: Fit view(s)/sheet(s) to a number of pixels across or down, or a zoom percentage of the real size at a resolution;
  • the options, as for printing: view links in blue, crop boundaries and unreferenced view tags hidden;
  • the Format of views without shading and of shaded views: PNG, JPEG, BMP or TIFF.

The 3D window is exported as it is shown, with its visual style.

docs.title: Floors, roofs, stairs and components
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs and railings are drawn in sketch mode: their lines are sketched first, and the element is made only when the sketch is finished. Components (furniture and plumbing fixtures) are placed with a click. Curtain walls are described in Walls, doors and windows.

docs.title: Sketch mode
docs.text:
Home ▸ Build ▸ Flooring, Roof, Stairs and Railing open sketch mode. The contextual tab is named after what is sketched (Edit | Create Floor Boundary, Create Roof Footprint, Create Stairs Sketch, Create Railing Path) and has:

  • the Mode panel: Finish Edit Mode makes the element; Cancel Edit Mode drops the sketch and leaves the model as it was;
  • the Draw panel, with the drawing tools of the element;
  • for stairs and railings, the Tools panel.

Nothing is made while sketching: the lines are magenta, and the model changes only with Finish Edit Mode. The whole element is then one step of the undo history: one Ctrl+Z takes it away.

docs.title: Drawing lines
docs.text:
Tool How it draws Line Click point after point: each click ends a line and starts the next. The length and angle of the line under the cursor are shown beside it; Shift keeps it horizontal or vertical. With Chain off on the options bar, each line is drawn on its own. Clicking the start of the chain again closes the loop Type a length and press Enter: the line ends that far along the cursor's direction (a stair's run too). Rectangle Two opposite corners: four lines Pick Walls Click a wall: its line is added to the sketch (see below). Press Tab over a wall, then click, to pick the whole chain of walls joined end to end Pick Lines Move over a wall, a grid, a line or the edge of a floor or roof: the line under the cursor is highlighted and named (a wall's faces, each layer boundary, its two Core Boundary lines and its axis); Tab goes to the next one there. Click to add a sketch line on it (set off by Offset towards the cursor) Slope Arrow Click the tail, then the head of the arrow (floors and roofs)

Offset on the options bar moves the drawn lines (and the lines of picked walls) by that distance.

Floors and roofs need closed loops. A loop drawn inside the outer one is an opening: the floor or the roof has a hole there. When Finish Edit Mode finds lines that do not close or that cross, a message says so and the sketch stays open to be fixed (Continue).

docs.title: Picking and changing sketch lines
docs.text:
Esc ends the chain being drawn; a second Esc puts the drawing tool down (so does Modify). While the sketch is open its lines are elements of the view, and Modify works on them as on other lines; nothing else can be picked until the sketch is finished:

  • the line under the cursor is highlighted; a click selects it, Ctrl adds lines, Shift takes them away, a window selects several, Tab the chain of joined lines;
  • the ends of the selected lines drag, and the ends joined there follow; a dragged line takes the lines joined to it along;
  • Move, Copy, Rotate, Mirror - Draw Axis, Array, Align, Offset, Trim/Extend to Corner and Split Element work on them, and the sketch stays open;
  • one selected line shows temporary dimensions to the nearest parallel line on each side (another sketch line, the wall's original outline, a wall, a grid, a level): click the value and type a distance to move the line; the symbol beside it makes a permanent dimension, kept while the sketch is open;
  • its properties are in the Properties palette: Defines Slope and Slope, for a roof line picked from a wall its Overhang, and its Length.

Align takes as its reference the line under the cursor, and Tab goes to the next one there, so a sketch line can be aligned to a wall's layer or core boundary. While drawing or dragging an end, the points snap to the corners of the walls' faces, layers and core boundaries, then onto those lines. Del deletes the selected lines. Ctrl+Z while sketching takes back the last change to the sketch, not to the model. All this works in plans, in sections and elevations (a wall's profile) and, for selecting, dragging ends and deleting, in the 3D view.

docs.title: Editing the sketch of an element
docs.text:
Select a floor, a roof, a stair or a railing: the Mode panel of its contextual tab has Edit Boundary (floors), Edit Footprint (roofs), Edit Sketch (stairs) or Edit Path (railings). Sketch mode opens with the element's lines, openings, slopes and arrow; Finish Edit Mode changes the same element, Cancel Edit Mode leaves it unchanged.

The sketch opens with Modify active: its lines can be selected and changed at once.

In a plan the sketch is drawn on the level; in the 3D view it lies on the element's own plane (the floor's top, the roof's base) and the 3D view stays open.

A new floor can be sketched in the 3D view too: Flooring started there puts the sketch on the plane of the level, the line being drawn follows the cursor with its length, and Finish Edit Mode makes the floor without leaving the 3D view. In the 3D view the options bar's Level chooses the work plane: the level whose plane the sketch lies on and the floor goes on. Pick Walls takes the wall whose face is under the cursor. Roofs by footprint, stairs and railings are sketched in a plan.

docs.title: Floors
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Flooring. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls.
  2. Click the walls around the floor, or press Tab over one of them and click to pick them all. Each line goes on the interior face of its wall; the lines of walls that meet are trimmed or extended to meet at the corner.
  3. Or draw the boundary with Line or Rectangle; draw a loop inside it for an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

On the options bar, Extend into wall (to core) puts picked lines into the wall up to the face of its core, and Offset moves them (a negative offset moves them away from the walls). The type of the new floor is the one in the type selector at the top of Properties.

docs.title: Sloped floors
docs.text:
A floor slopes in one direction, set in one of two ways while sketching:

  • a Slope Arrow: its properties are Specify (Height at Tail, from the heights of its two ends, or Slope), Height Offset at Tail, Height Offset at Head and Slope. The heights are measured from the top of the floor;
  • one boundary line with Defines Slope ticked and its Slope in degrees: the floor rises from that line, inwards.

The floor is sloped in 3D and in sections. Its Slope Angle in Properties changes the slope afterwards.

docs.title: Floors over walls
docs.text: When a floor crosses walls (an upper floor resting on the walls below, for instance), its slab is cut out of them: in 3D and in sections the wall stops under the floor and goes on above it, and walls go on through the floor's openings.

docs.title: Floor properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Level, Height Offset From Level The level and the height of the top face from it Slope Angle The slope of a sloped floor, in degrees Thickness From the type's layers (read-only) Perimeter, Area, Volume Without the openings (read-only) Comments, Mark Free text

Type Properties has the floor's Structure (its layers) and its default thickness.

docs.title: Roofs
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Roof. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls; the options bar has Defines Slope, Overhang and Extend into wall (to core).
  2. Pick the walls (Tab for the whole chain). Each line goes on the exterior face of its wall, moved out by the overhang (from the face of the core with Extend into wall (to core)).
  3. Or draw the footprint with Line or Rectangle; a loop inside is an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

Every line with Defines Slope rises inwards at its Slope (30° by default); a small triangle with the slope is drawn beside it. The shape comes from those lines:

  • all the lines define the slope: a hip roof;
  • two opposite lines do not: a gable roof, the walls under the gables rise to the ridge when attached;
  • no line defines the slope: a flat roof, or a roof sloping along a Slope Arrow (then no line may define a slope).

To change one line, press Esc twice, click the line and change Defines Roof Slope, Slope or (lines picked from walls) Overhang in Properties.

Select walls, click Modify Wall ▸ Attach Top/Base, then the roof: they rise to its underside, gables included (Walls, doors and windows tells more).

docs.title: Roof properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Base Level, Base Offset From Level Where the eaves are: by default on top of the walls of the level Slope The slope of every line that defines one (or of the arrow) Thickness, Maximum Ridge Height, Area, Volume Read-only Comments, Mark Free text

In plan a roof shows its outline, ridges and hips; in 3D its slopes, overhangs and layers.

docs.title: Stairs
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Circulation ▸ Stairs. Sketch mode starts with Run.
  2. Click where the first riser is, then where the run ends: the run snaps to whole treads, and the status bar counts the risers made and left (for example 9 risers created, 8 remaining).
  3. To turn, click again away from the end of the first run and draw the next one: a landing joins them.
  4. When every riser is placed, click Finish Edit Mode.

The Width on the options bar is that of the new stair (by default the type's). Tools ▸ Railing Type chooses the railings of the new stair: a railing type, put on both sides, or None.

The number of risers comes from the height between Base Level and Top Level (with their offsets) and the type's Maximum Riser Height; changing a level or an offset in Properties changes the risers. Edit Sketch reopens the runs: delete a run (click it, Del) and draw it again; the railings of the stair follow.

In plan the stair shows its treads up to the cut line, the break line, the arrow and the UP/DN text; in 3D its treads and risers, or a monolithic slab, its landings and railings.

docs.title: How a stair is built
docs.text:
Type Properties of the stair decide its construction:

  • Monolithic Stairs ticked: each run is a concrete slab cut to the steps; its underside runs parallel to the slope, Structural Depth below the inner corners of the steps, and the landings are as thick: the sloping underside of a run meets the landing's underside along a line, without a step; each run ends with its last tread: the landing, flush with it, or the floor above makes the last riser, so steps and slab show as one solid with no line across the risers.
  • otherwise treads (Tread Thickness) with risers (Riser Type Straight, Riser Thickness) or open (None), on stringers: Right Stringer and Left Stringer Closed (a board the treads are housed in), Open (a board cut to the steps, the treads on top) or None, and Middle Stringers under the treads, with their Stringer Thickness and Stringer Height.

The landing stops behind the last riser of the run that reaches it, following its back face; in a monolithic stair it starts at the riser's face. At the top the run's underside goes on under the floor of the top level until it meets the floor's underside, as under a landing.

A section across the stair shows it cut with its slab. Volume in Properties and in the schedule of stairs is the volume of its solids.

docs.title: Railings
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Circulation ▸ Railing.
  2. Draw the path with Line: one chain of connected lines (a path in pieces is refused at Finish Edit Mode).
  3. To put the railing on a stair, click Tools ▸ Pick New Host and then the stair: the path drawn on it climbs with the stair.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

Edit Path reopens the path of a railing. The railing's Type Properties has its Railing Height and Baluster Spacing: changing them changes every railing of that type.

The railings of a stair run on over its landings as one rail, at their height above the line of the nosings and above the landings. Where a run leaves a landing one riser higher, the type's Tangent Joins (the rail goes straight on) and Angled Joins (it turns) decide the join: Extend Rails to Meet (tangent joins only) carries the sloping rail on down to the landing, Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments rises upright at the first riser, No Connector leaves a gap.

The rails are mitred at every joint, where the path turns and where the slope changes: with Rail Connections Weld each rail is one piece, with Trim its pieces are cut on the joint's vertical plane. A post stands at the start and the end of each railing and at every change of direction in plan (none where only the slope changes). Use Landing Height Adjustment with Landing Height Adjustment raises (or lowers) the rail over the landings by that much.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Component. The type selector lists the components loaded in the project; a preview follows the cursor, in plan and in the 3D view.
  2. Press Space to turn the preview by 90°.
  3. Click to place the component on the level of the plan.

Mode ▸ Load Family opens the library, by folder (Furniture, Plumbing Fixtures): choose a family and click Open to add its types to the project.

Select a component and click Host ▸ Pick New Host, then a floor: the component moves onto the floor and stays on its top (click an empty point to put it back on the level). Its properties are Level, Host, Offset from Level, Rotation, Mark and Comments; Type Properties has its width, depth, height and material.

docs.title: Schedules and IFC
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs, railings and furniture have their schedules (View ▸ Create ▸ Schedules ▸ Schedule/Quantities), one row per element. Export ▸ Export IFC4… writes floors as slabs (with their openings and slopes), roofs, stairs with their flights and landings, railings, furniture and plumbing fixtures.

docs.title: Not yet in BIMopen
docs.text: Ceilings, ramps, roofs by extrusion, shafts and vertical openings, slab edges, fascias, gutters and soffits, stairs sketched by boundary and riser lines, spiral stairs, and arcs in sketches come after this chapter's realignment.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This chapter shows how to start BIMopen on the desktop and in the browser, what the sample project contains, and how to model a first small house: four walls, a door, a window, a floor, a roof, a 3D view and a sheet with the plan on it. It takes about ten minutes.

docs.title: Running BIMopen on the desktop
docs.text:
BIMopen is built from its source code with Rust, version 1.90 or later. On Linux the graphical interface also needs the development files of xkbcommon, Wayland and GTK 3.

sudo apt-get install -y libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev libgtk-3-dev   # Debian, Ubuntu
cargo run --release -p bimopen -- --sample                             # opens the sample house

The program is bimopen. It accepts a file to open and one option:

Command What it opens bimopen A new, empty project bimopen --sample The sample house bimopen house.bimopen The project saved in house.bimopen

You can also open a project by dragging a .bimopen file from the file manager into the window.

docs.title: Language and theme
docs.text:
The first time, BIMopen speaks the language of the operating system when it is one of its six languages (Italian, English, German, French, Spanish, Arabic), and English otherwise. To change it, use the language menu at the right end of the title bar (the globe with the language's name), or Application menu ▸ Options ▸ Language. The interface changes at once.

In Options you also choose the Theme, Light or Dark, and whether the background of the views is inverted (Invert background color: dark views with light lines). Choosing the dark theme also inverts the background; you can turn it back off. BIMopen remembers the language and the theme for the next time.

docs.title: Running BIMopen in the browser
docs.text:
The web version is the same program, compiled for the browser. Open atsanna.github.io/bimopen-site/app/: it starts with the sample house. Nothing needs to be installed, and the project stays in your browser: it is not sent anywhere.

The address accepts these options, which can be combined with &:

Address Effect app/?lang=de Opens in German for this visit (it, en, de, fr, es, ar) app/?empty Starts with a new, empty project instead of the sample app/?webgl Draws with WebGL2 even where WebGPU is available

The browser must support WebGPU or WebGL2. In the browser some things work differently:

  • Open… cannot show a file dialog: drag a .bimopen file into the page to open it;
  • Save and the exports download the file, with the name of the project.

To build the web version yourself:

cargo xtask web                              # builds dist/web
python3 -m http.server 8080 -d dist/web      # then open http://localhost:8080

cargo xtask web needs the wasm32-unknown-unknown target of Rust and the wasm-bindgen command of the version written in Cargo.lock; with binaryen's wasm-opt installed, the result is smaller.

docs.title: The sample project
docs.text:
The sample house shows most of what BIMopen can do. Open it with Application menu ▸ Sample project, with bimopen --sample, or by typing sample at the command line.

It contains:

  • two levels, each with its floor plan, and five grid lines;
  • fifteen walls of four types, with layers, joined at the corners;
  • six doors and twelve windows, tagged in the plans;
  • two floors, a pitched roof, a stair with its railings and a storefront curtain wall;
  • furniture and plumbing fixtures, eight rooms coloured by use, with a legend;
  • a section, an elevation, an area plan, a saved 3D view and a drafting view with a wall detail;
  • dimensions, text notes and the schedules of walls, doors, windows, rooms and materials.

Tip

The sample is a good place to try a tool before using it on your own project: a new sample is always one click away, and nothing you change in it is saved unless you save it.

docs.title: Your first house
docs.text: The steps below start from an empty project and end with a sheet. Every step names the button to click; the interface chapter explains each part of the window.

docs.title: 1. Start a new project
docs.text:
1. Click the blue B button at the left end of the title bar: the application menu opens.
  2. Click New ▸ Project…. The New project dialog proposes BIMopen's default template: click OK.

The new project has two levels, Ground Floor and First Floor, a floor plan for each, and the default 3D view. It has no walls yet. Its wall, door, window, floor and roof types are ready to use.

docs.title: 2. Open the ground floor plan
docs.text:
In the Project Browser, under Views (all) ▸ Floor Plans, double-click Ground Floor. The plan opens in the drawing area and the title bar shows Floor Plan: Ground Floor.

Note

A single click on a view in the Project Browser shows its properties in the Properties palette without opening it. A double-click opens it.

docs.title: 3. Draw four walls
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Wall. The ribbon switches to the contextual tab Edit | Place Wall, the options bar shows the settings of the wall, and Properties shows the type of the next wall, Exterior wall - Clay block 300 + ETICS.
  2. On the options bar, turn on Ortho (Shift): the walls stay horizontal or vertical.
  3. Click in the plan where the first corner goes. The command line asks for the next point: WALL next point [Esc to finish]:.
  4. Click the second, third and fourth corners. While you move the mouse, the length and the angle of the wall being drawn are shown next to it.
  5. Click the first corner again: the four walls are joined at the corners.
  6. Press Esc to stop the chain, and Esc again to end the tool.

Tip

You can draw the same walls by typing their corners in metres: wall 0,0 10,0 10,6 0,6 c. The final c closes the chain. See Command line and MCP.

docs.title: 4. Add a door and a window
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Door, then click on a wall where the door goes. The door is placed in the wall, which is cut around it. The command line confirms it: Door «Single swing door 80x210» in wall ….
  2. Press Esc: the tool ends and the ribbon returns to the Home tab.
  3. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Window, click on another wall, and press Esc.

A door or a window can only be placed in a wall: after a click away from the walls, the command line answers no wall at that point and nothing is placed.

docs.title: 5. Add a floor and a roof
docs.text:
1. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Flooring. Sketch mode opens: the contextual tab Edit | Create Floor Boundary, with Pick Walls active.
  2. Move the cursor over a wall and press Tab: the four walls are highlighted. Click: their lines go on the inner faces of the walls.
  3. Click Finish Edit Mode: the floor is made and the command line gives its area.
  4. Click Home ▸ Build ▸ Roof. Pick Walls is active again; the options bar has Defines Slope (ticked) and the Overhang (500 mm by default).
  5. Press Tab over a wall, click, then Finish Edit Mode: a hip roof sloping at 30° covers the walls, with the overhang all around.

Floors, roofs, stairs and components tells more about sketch mode.

docs.title: 6. Look at it in 3D
docs.text: Click the 3D View button (the cube) on the quick access toolbar. The default 3D view, {3D}, opens. Drag with the right mouse button (or with Shift and the middle button) to orbit, drag with the middle button to pan, and turn the wheel to zoom; the left button selects, as in plans. Home fits the whole model in the view.

docs.title: 7. Put the plan on a sheet
docs.text:
1. Click the View tab, then Sheet Composition ▸ Sheet. The New Sheet dialog lists the title blocks: none, A0, A1, A2 or A3, with their size in millimetres.
  2. Click OK. The sheet is created with the next free number (A101 for the first one, then A102…) and opens.
  3. Click Sheet Composition ▸ View. The Views dialog lists the views that are not on a sheet yet.
  4. Choose Floor Plan: Ground Floor and click Add View to Sheet. A rectangle of the plan's size follows the cursor: click on the sheet where the plan goes. It is placed at its own scale, 1 : 100, as a viewport, which stays selected.

docs.title: 8. Undo, redo and save
docs.text:
• Ctrl+Z undoes the last change (here, the viewport goes away); Ctrl+Y redoes it. The arrows of the quick access toolbar do the same.
  • Ctrl+S saves the project. A project that has never been saved asks for a file name first; the file has the extension .bimopen. In the browser, the file is downloaded.

The title bar shows an asterisk after the project's name while there are unsaved changes: Untitled project *.

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• The interface describes every part of the window.
  • Keyboard shortcuts lists the keys and the two-letter shortcuts, such as WA for a wall.
  • Command line and MCP shows how to type commands, run scripts and let an agent model for you.

docs.title: Interface styles
docs.text:
BIMopen has two interface styles. Both run the same commands, with the same names, keyboard shortcuts and results; only the look and the place of the tools change.

  • The Revit style, described in The interface: the ribbon, the options bar, the Properties palette and the Project Browser. BIMopen starts in this style.
  • The BIMopen style: a side rail, a command search, tool cards, tools floating over the view, an element panel with tabs and a strip of view thumbnails.

docs.title: Choosing the style
docs.text:
1. Open the application menu and choose Options (in the BIMopen style, the gear at the right end of the top bar).
  2. Under User Interface, set Interface to Revit or BIMopen.

The window changes at once. The choice is remembered, on the desktop and in the browser, and the next session starts in the same style. Theme (Light or Dark) applies to both styles.

docs.title: The BIMopen style
docs.text:
Part Where What it holds Rail Left edge BIMopen's mark (the application menu), Home (the project), Create, Document, View, Coordinate, the open project and Settings. They take the place of the ribbon's tabs. A click on the selected entry folds the tool panel Top bar Top The project and the active view, the command search, undo and redo, the save state, the light or dark theme, the ? menu and Options Tool panel Left, beside the rail The ribbon's tabs as groups of tiles, each command once: Create has Home and Insert (with the Architecture tab), Document the sheets and Annotate, View the View tab and the Project Browser, Coordinate Inquiry, Settings Manage. While a tool works or something is selected, the contextual tab («Modify | Walls»: move, copy, rotate, mirror, trim, align, edit profile, Finish Edit Mode…) sits on top; Esc or a click on empty space takes it away Options strip Over the view, while a tool works The options of the tool (height, location line, chain…), the options bar of the Revit style View Centre The view selector and + for a new view. One view bar, bottom centre: select, the Pan, Orbit (3D) and Zoom modes (with one on, the left button drags the view; Esc ends it), zoom to fit, Zoom Options, SteeringWheels (3D) | the visual style, the detail level, Sun and shadows (3D), Crop (crop view, show the crop region), Temporary Hide/Isolate (its menu, as the view control bar's; the view is framed while it is on) and Reveal Hidden Elements | full screen. In 3D views the ViewCube (a click on a face, an edge or a corner looks from there, a drag orbits, the house goes back to the starting view); on the selection, the move arrows (drag one to move along it, the centre to move freely in plan: the distance shows as you drag, the release moves as Move does) Element panel Right The selected element: Properties (the same parameters as the Properties palette), Materials (the layers of its type with their colours and thicknesses, and a layered preview), Classification (category, type, IFC class) and Relations (level, host, hosted doors and windows, views and schedules). With nothing selected, the properties of the active view View strip Under the view The views by kind (Views, Plans, Sections, Elevations, 3D, Sheets, Schedules) as thumbnails or as a list; a click opens the view, + makes a new one Status bar Bottom The project and the version, the active view, the prompt of the active tool, the cursor coordinates, the active level (its menu opens the plan of another level), the selection count (it opens Filter), the Select and Drag, Snap, Grid and Ortho switches, the scale of the view and the command log

The Structure and MEP tabs of Create say that these disciplines are not in BIMopen yet.

docs.title: Command search
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+K, or click the search box in the top bar, and type a few letters: the list shows the commands, views, sheets, schedules, elements and materials that match. Click a result, or choose it with the arrow keys and press Enter: a command starts, a view opens, an element is selected and shown, a material opens in Materials. The search finds every command of the ribbon's tabs, the contextual tab's too (with a view selected on a sheet, «activate» finds Activate View), and runs it as its button does.

The search box is also the command line of the style. Typing in a view writes there, as the command line does in the Revit style, and Enter runs a keyboard shortcut (WA, DR, ZF…) or a command with its arguments (wall 0,0 5,0) as typed. The list of commands is in Command line and MCP.

docs.title: Right-click menu
docs.text: In plans, sections and 3D views the right button opens a dark menu: with a selection, the modify commands first (Move, Copy, Rotate, Align, Offset and the others), then the same items as the view's menu in the Revit style.

docs.title: Everything of the Revit style
docs.text:
Every function of the Revit style is in the BIMopen style, once:

  • every button of the ribbon is a tile of the tool panel, in the rail entry that holds its tab, and the contextual Modify tab sits on top of the panel while a tool works or something is selected;
  • BIMopen's mark at the top of the rail opens the application menu; the top bar has undo, redo and the ? menu;
  • View holds the whole Project Browser, with its menus;
  • a thumbnail of the view strip can be dragged onto the open sheet, or onto a sheet's thumbnail, and its right-click menu has the browser's actions and Open in the active window;
  • the view selector's menu arranges the view windows (Switch Windows, Tile, Cascade, Maximize, Replicate, Close Hidden); Ctrl+Tab goes to the previous window;
  • the right button on a tile offers Add to Quick Access Toolbar: the tool shows in the top bar, works from any section of the rail, and its right button offers Remove from Quick Access Toolbar;
  • the key tips work as on the ribbon: tap Alt (or press F10), then a tab's letter opens the rail section that holds it (its letter shows on the rail) and a tool's letters start it.

docs.title: Light and dark
docs.text: In Arabic the whole window is mirrored, in both styles: the rail and the tool panel are on the right, the element panel on the left.

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
The BIMopen window has the same parts in the desktop and in the web version. From top to bottom:

  1. the title bar, with the application menu, the quick access toolbar, the name of the project and of the active view, the language menu and the help menu;
  2. the ribbon, with its tabs and panels of tools;
  3. the options bar, with the settings of the active tool;
  4. on the left, the Properties palette above the Project Browser;
  5. the drawing area, where the views open in windows, each with its view control bar;
  6. the command line, with the log of what has been done;
  7. the status bar.

The palettes keep their width whatever they show: a long name is cut with «…» and its tooltip shows it whole. Drag the edge of the palettes to make them wider or narrower, and the line between Properties and the Project Browser to share the height; BIMopen remembers both for the next session. In the BIMopen style the tool panel and the element panel work the same way.

In Arabic the whole window is mirrored: the palettes are on the right, the ribbon and the options bar read from right to left, and the navigation bar is on the left edge of the views.

docs.title: Application menu
docs.text:
The blue B button at the left end of the title bar opens the application menu: the commands that work on the whole project.

Item What it does New Closes the current project and starts a new one from the default template: two levels with their plans, and the default types Open… Opens a .bimopen project, or imports an .rvt model, chosen in a file dialog. In the browser, drag the file into the page instead Sample project Opens the sample house Save Ctrl+S Saves the project in its file; a project never saved asks for a name, like Save As… Save As… Saves the project in a new .bimopen file and goes on working on that file Print… Ctrl+P Prints sheets to PDF Export ▸ Export IFC4… Writes the model as an IFC4 file Export ▸ Export plan SVG… Writes the active plan as an SVG drawing Export ▸ Export view PNG… Writes the active view as a PNG image Open Documents Lists the open view windows; click one to bring it to the front Options Opens the Options dialog Exit Closes BIMopen (desktop only)

New, Open… and Sample project replace the current project without asking: save it first if you want to keep it.

Warning

Unsaved changes are lost when you choose New, Open… or Sample project. The asterisk after the project's name in the title bar tells you that there are unsaved changes.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Application menu ▸ Options has two groups:

Setting Values Effect User Interface ▸ Language Italiano, English, Deutsch, Français, Español, العربية The language of the whole interface, at once User Interface ▸ Theme Light, Dark The colours of the window. Dark also turns on Invert background color Graphics ▸ Invert background color on, off Views with a dark background and light lines

BIMopen remembers the language and the theme the next time it starts.

docs.title: Quick access toolbar
docs.text:
Next to the application menu, the quick access toolbar keeps the most used commands one click away. Rest the mouse on a button to read what it does and its shortcut.

Button What it does Open… (folder) As in the application menu Save (disk) Saves, Ctrl+S Undo (arrow left) Undoes the last change, Ctrl+Z. Greyed when there is nothing to undo Redo (arrow right) Redoes the change just undone, Ctrl+Y. Greyed when there is nothing to redo Aligned dimension Starts the aligned dimension tool, DI Tag by Category Starts Tag by Category, as on Annotate ▸ Tag: click an element to tag it, TG Text Starts the text tool, TX 3D View (cube) Opens the default 3D view, {3D} Section Starts the section tool, SE Close Hidden Closes every view window except the active one. Greyed when only one is open Switch Windows Lists the open view windows; the active one is ticked

In the middle of the title bar, when the window is wide enough, BIMopen shows the name of the project and of the active view, for example Sample house — BIMopen - Floor Plan: Ground Floor. An asterisk after the project's name means that it has unsaved changes.

At the right end:
